Archive item 1: Warehouse Staff Survey – Perceptions and Suggestions
Source format: survey responses

**Section 2: Training and Support**

Responses regarding training were mixed. When asked whether they had received adequate training for their current role, 26 staff agreed, 12 were neutral, and 9 disagreed. Several of those who disagreed mentioned that they had not received refresher training on the new pallet wrapping machine that was installed in late January. One comment said: "The new wrapper is good but nobody showed me the settings. I just press the green button and hope."

There were also requests for more training on cold-chain handling procedures. A recurring theme in the comments was that staff wanted clearer guidance on how long product can sit on the dock before being moved into the chiller. One respondent wrote: "We need a refresher on the cold chain rules. Some of the new guys don't know the limits." Another comment suggested that a short toolbox talk on temperature monitoring would be useful before the winter season.

Several staff expressed interest in cross-training opportunities, particularly for the inventory control role. One comment noted: "I would like to learn how to do cycle counts so I can help out when someone is on leave." Another respondent mentioned that the training book in the lunchroom is out of date and that the pages for the electric pallet jack are missing.

**Section 3: Facility Conditions and Equipment**

The facility conditions section received the most varied responses. Staff generally agreed that the warehouse is clean and well-maintained, with 33 of 47 selecting "Agree" or "Strongly Agree" for the statement "The facility is kept clean and tidy." However, there were several comments about the condition of the staff amenities. One comment read: "The shower in the male change room has been blocked for a week. Someone put a sign on it but nothing has happened." Another mentioned that the drinking water tap near the dispatch office is slow and that staff often have to walk to the other end of the building for a refill.

Hobart Regional Distribution Centre has_temperature_range 2.0 to 4.0 degrees Celsius. Record status: current.

Equipment reliability was a common topic. Several respondents noted that one of the reach trucks in the freezer aisle has a squeaky brake and that it sometimes jerks when stopping. One comment said: "The yellow reach truck needs a service. It makes a loud noise and the brake feels slack." Another comment mentioned that the temperature probe used for checking inbound pallets is sometimes hard to read because the screen is scratched.

A few staff commented on the lighting in the packing area, noting that one of the fluorescent tubes flickers. One respondent wrote: "The light near bay 4 flickers all day. It gives me a headache." There was also a suggestion to install a second fan in the break room, as the room gets warm during the afternoon.

**Section 4: Temperature and Cold-Chain Perceptions**

This section asked staff about their general perceptions of temperature management in the facility. Comments were generally positive, but several respondents noted that they sometimes see product sitting on the dock for longer than they expect. One comment read: "Sometimes the pallets wait on the dock while we are short staffed. I know there is a limit but I am not sure what it is." Another respondent wrote: "The chiller feels cold enough, but I worry about summer days when the dock door is open for a long time."

A number of staff mentioned that they would like to see the temperature readouts from the chiller displayed more prominently in the work area. One comment said: "We have to walk to the office to check the temp. It would be good to have a screen on the floor." Another respondent noted that the temperature log sheet near the chiller door is sometimes not filled in, particularly on the weekend shift.

The current temperature range for the main chiller at the Hobart Regional Distribution Centre is 2.0 to 4.0 degrees Celsius. This is the current controlled entry under the Cold Chain Integrity Policy. Several staff commented that they were aware of this range, but that they were unsure about the procedures for reporting a temperature excursion. One comment read: "I know the range is 2 to 4, but what do we do if it goes above that? I have never seen it happen, but I would not know who to call."
Respondents were asked whether they had submitted a maintenance request in the past three months, and if so, how long it took for the issue to be addressed.

- 22 staff said they had submitted at least one maintenance request.
- Of those, 9 said the issue was fixed within a week.
- 7 said it took between one and two weeks.
- 4 said it took more than two weeks.
- 2 said the issue was still outstanding at the time of the survey.

One respondent commented: "I put in a request for the fan in the freezer anteroom in early January. It is still not fixed. The motor whines and I worry it will stop completely." Another wrote: "The tap in the wash bay drips. I reported it before Christmas and it got fixed in the second week of January, so that was okay."

A few staff noted that they were not sure how to check the status of a maintenance request once it had been submitted. One comment read: "I hand my form to the supervisor and I never hear anything back. It would be good to know if it has been logged properly."

**Section 7: Training and Procedures**

This section asked staff about their familiarity with standard operating procedures, particularly those related to cold-chain integrity and equipment handling.

When asked about the Cold Chain Integrity Policy, 14 respondents said they were "very familiar" with it, 12 said "somewhat familiar," and 6 said they were "not very familiar." A few comments suggested that refresher training would be useful, especially for staff who had joined in the past year.

One respondent wrote: "I came in October and I got shown the chiller once. I know the basics but I would not feel confident handling a temperature excursion on my own." Another comment said: "The SOP for loading the truck is clear, but the one for the dock leveller is outdated. It does not mention the new safety gate."

There were also a few comments about the temperature log sheet near the chiller door. Several staff said that the sheet is sometimes not filled in, particularly on the weekend shift, and that they were unsure whose responsibility it was to check it.

**Section 8: General Comments**

The final section of the survey gave staff the opportunity to provide any other comments. The responses covered a range of topics, including workload, communication, and the upcoming Hobart Show Day public holiday.

On workload, one respondent wrote: "We have been short staffed on the afternoon shift for three weeks. Everyone is doing double duty and it is starting to show." Another comment said: "The morning crew is fine, but the afternoon crew is always behind because the dock gets busy after lunch."

On communication, a few staff mentioned that they would like more regular updates from the shift supervisor. One comment read: "We only hear about changes when something goes wrong. It would be good to have a quick huddle at the start of the shift, even if it is just five minutes."

One respondent raised a concern about the upcoming Hobart Show Day public holiday, noting that the roster had not been published yet and that staff were unsure whether they would be working. Another comment mentioned that the break room gets warm during the afternoon and suggested installing a second fan.

A handful of responses were positive. One staff member wrote: "The team is good and we look after each other. The new reach truck is much easier to drive than the old one." Another said: "I have been here for six years and the place has improved a lot. The chiller is reliable and we rarely have issues with the temperature."

**Section 9: Summary of Key Findings**

The survey responses indicate that staff are generally satisfied with the overall operation of the warehouse, but there are several areas where improvements could be made. The most frequently mentioned issues were:

1. The dock leveller at bay 2, which has been reported as faulty by multiple staff members.
2. The scratched screen on the handheld temperature probe.
3. The flickering light near bay 4 in the packing area.
4. The lack of visibility of temperature readouts from the chiller.
5. Uncertainty about the procedure for reporting a temperature excursion.
6. Inconsistent completion of the temperature log sheet, particularly on weekends.
7. Delays in addressing some maintenance requests.
8. A desire for more regular communication from the shift supervisor.
Another respondent raised a question about communication: "Why do we never hear about the contracts? The staff are the ones who deal with the suppliers every day. We should be told if something is changing. I heard the co‑op contract is current until the end of June this year, but I do not know what happens after that."

A shorter comment read: "The co‑op is good. Keep them."

One response mentioned the quality of produce: "The co‑op fruit and veg is always fresh. The apples are better than the ones from the mainland. I hope the contract continues."

A further comment said: "I am not sure who decides which suppliers we use, but the co‑op has never given us a problem. The paperwork is always in order and the deliveries are on time."

One respondent expressed concern about the future: "If the co‑op contract is not renewed, the afternoon shift will be worse. They are the only ones who deliver after 2 pm and the dock gets busy. I would like to know what the plan is."

Another comment noted: "The co‑op drivers know our layout. They do not need directions anymore. That saves us time."

One response suggested: "Maybe we should have a meeting with the co‑op before the contract expires. It would be good to talk about the delivery times and the temperature checks. I think the contract is current, but I am not sure when it finishes."

A final comment in this area said: "I do not have any complaints about the co‑op. They are better than the last supplier. I just hope we do not go back to the old arrangement."

**Section 11: Training and Skill Development**

When asked about training, the majority of respondents (34 out of 47) said they had received enough training to do their job safely. However, several comments indicated a desire for more specific training.

One respondent wrote: "I would like to do a refresher on the reach truck. I have not driven one for a while and I am not confident."

Another said: "The new handheld temp probe is good, but the screen is scratched and hard to read in the light. I have asked for a replacement twice. It would be good if we could have a short session on how to use the probe properly, because some staff do not know how to log the readings."

A third comment mentioned: "I have been here for two years and I have never been shown how to do the temperature excursion report. I know we are supposed to fill it in, but I do not know where the forms are."

One respondent suggested: "It would be good to have a training session on the chiller alarms. I do not know what to do if the alarm goes off at night."

Another comment said: "The new staff are not trained properly on the dock. They do not know how to stack the pallets and they leave gaps. We need a proper induction."

A further response noted: "I would like to learn how to use the computer system for the inventory. I am only on the dock, but it would help if I could check the stock levels myself."

One respondent wrote: "The training is fine, but we never get a follow‑up. I did the first aid course three years ago and I have not done a refresher since."

**Section 12: General Comments and Suggestions**

The final section of the survey invited any other comments. Responses varied widely.

One respondent wrote: "The coffee machine in the break room has been broken for two weeks. I have reported it, but nothing has happened. It is a small thing, but it makes a difference."

Another said: "The car park is too small. People park on the grass and it gets muddy in the rain. We need more spaces or a better layout."

A third comment read: "The uniform is not warm enough for the chiller. I have to wear my own jumper underneath and it is not the right colour. Can we get better jackets?"

One respondent noted: "The toilet on the dock is out of order again. It has been like that for a month. We have to walk all the way to the front office."

Another comment said: "I appreciate that we get paid on time and the shifts are regular. It is a good place to work overall."

One respondent wrote: "The afternoon shift is always short staffed. I have mentioned this before, but nothing has changed. We need at least two more people."
**Warehouse Staff Survey – Perceptions and Suggestions (continued)**

**Section 13: Safety and Communication**

When asked about safety in the workplace, most respondents rated the overall conditions as acceptable, though several raised specific concerns about the dock area and the chiller.

One respondent commented: "The floor near the freezer door is always wet. I have slipped twice this month. We need a mat or something to dry it."

Another said: "The safety talk at the start of shift is good, but it is always the same. We hear the same thing every day and people stop listening."

A third response read: "The first aid kit on the dock is never full. I checked it last week and there was no bandage left. The checklist says it is checked every Monday, but I am not sure who does it."

One respondent noted: "The forklift drivers are careful, but the new guy on the afternoon shift drives too fast. I have told the supervisor twice, but nothing has been done."

Another comment said: "We had a good safety meeting last month about the cold chain. It was useful to go over the temperature rules again. We should do that more often."

On communication, responses were mixed. Several staff said they felt informed about shift changes, but many wanted more notice.

One respondent wrote: "The roster comes out on Friday afternoon for the next week. It is hard to plan anything. Can we get it earlier?"

Another said: "The supervisors are good at telling us what to do, but nobody tells us why. It would help to know the bigger picture."

A third comment read: "I found out about the new pallet racking from a mate on the other shift. Nobody told us in a meeting. It would be good to hear it from the boss."

One respondent noted: "The noticeboard near the time clock is out of date. There is still a notice about the Christmas party. We need someone to keep it current."

Another said: "I like the morning huddle. It is short and we get the important stuff. But sometimes it is too loud near the dock to hear."

**Section 14: Morale and Workplace Culture**

Responses on morale were generally positive, with several staff commenting that they felt part of a team. However, a few raised concerns about fairness and recognition.

One respondent wrote: "The crew on the day shift gets along well. We help each other out. That is why I stay."

Another said: "The supervisors say thanks when we do a good job, but it does not go further than that. There is no bonus or even a mention in the newsletter."

A third comment read: "Some people get the easy jobs every day. It is the same few who always get the nice work and the rest of us do the hard stuff. It does not feel fair."

One respondent noted: "The last few months have been busy with the new season. Everyone is tired, but we are pulling together. A bit of overtime would help."

Another said: "I do not mind the work, but the music in the packing area is too loud. Some of us like it quiet. Can we have a vote?"

One respondent wrote: "The staff are good. The job is fine. It is just the little things that could be better, like the break room and the toilets."

A further comment read: "I have been here for three years and I have never had a performance review. I do not know if I am doing well or not. It would be good to know."

One respondent said: "The afternoon shift is always short staffed. I have mentioned this before, but nothing has changed. We need at least two more people."

**Section 15: Additional Comments**

The final open section of the survey gave staff the chance to add anything not covered elsewhere. Many responses repeated earlier themes, but a few new points emerged.

One respondent wrote: "The delivery drivers from the transport company are sometimes rude. They do not wait for us to check the load and they leave the dock in a hurry. It makes our job harder."

Another said: "The radio on the dock is broken. We use it to call the office when we need a hand. It has been off for a week. Can we get it fixed?"

A third comment read: "I would like to see more variety in the work. I have been on the same station for six months. It gets boring."

documents.title: Warehouse Staff Survey – Perceptions and Suggestions
documents.content:
**Section 2: Training and Support**

Responses regarding training were mixed. When asked whether they had received adequate training for their current role, 26 staff agreed, 12 were neutral, and 9 disagreed. Several of those who disagreed mentioned that they had not received refresher training on the new pallet wrapping machine that was installed in late January. One comment said: "The new wrapper is good but nobody showed me the settings. I just press the green button and hope."

There were also requests for more training on cold-chain handling procedures. A recurring theme in the comments was that staff wanted clearer guidance on how long product can sit on the dock before being moved into the chiller. One respondent wrote: "We need a refresher on the cold chain rules. Some of the new guys don't know the limits." Another comment suggested that a short toolbox talk on temperature monitoring would be useful before the winter season.

Several staff expressed interest in cross-training opportunities, particularly for the inventory control role. One comment noted: "I would like to learn how to do cycle counts so I can help out when someone is on leave." Another respondent mentioned that the training book in the lunchroom is out of date and that the pages for the electric pallet jack are missing.

**Section 3: Facility Conditions and Equipment**

The facility conditions section received the most varied responses. Staff generally agreed that the warehouse is clean and well-maintained, with 33 of 47 selecting "Agree" or "Strongly Agree" for the statement "The facility is kept clean and tidy." However, there were several comments about the condition of the staff amenities. One comment read: "The shower in the male change room has been blocked for a week. Someone put a sign on it but nothing has happened." Another mentioned that the drinking water tap near the dispatch office is slow and that staff often have to walk to the other end of the building for a refill.

Hobart Regional Distribution Centre has_temperature_range 2.0 to 4.0 degrees Celsius. Record status: current.

Equipment reliability was a common topic. Several respondents noted that one of the reach trucks in the freezer aisle has a squeaky brake and that it sometimes jerks when stopping. One comment said: "The yellow reach truck needs a service. It makes a loud noise and the brake feels slack." Another comment mentioned that the temperature probe used for checking inbound pallets is sometimes hard to read because the screen is scratched.

A few staff commented on the lighting in the packing area, noting that one of the fluorescent tubes flickers. One respondent wrote: "The light near bay 4 flickers all day. It gives me a headache." There was also a suggestion to install a second fan in the break room, as the room gets warm during the afternoon.

**Section 4: Temperature and Cold-Chain Perceptions**

This section asked staff about their general perceptions of temperature management in the facility. Comments were generally positive, but several respondents noted that they sometimes see product sitting on the dock for longer than they expect. One comment read: "Sometimes the pallets wait on the dock while we are short staffed. I know there is a limit but I am not sure what it is." Another respondent wrote: "The chiller feels cold enough, but I worry about summer days when the dock door is open for a long time."

A number of staff mentioned that they would like to see the temperature readouts from the chiller displayed more prominently in the work area. One comment said: "We have to walk to the office to check the temp. It would be good to have a screen on the floor." Another respondent noted that the temperature log sheet near the chiller door is sometimes not filled in, particularly on the weekend shift.

The current temperature range for the main chiller at the Hobart Regional Distribution Centre is 2.0 to 4.0 degrees Celsius. This is the current controlled entry under the Cold Chain Integrity Policy. Several staff commented that they were aware of this range, but that they were unsure about the procedures for reporting a temperature excursion. One comment read: "I know the range is 2 to 4, but what do we do if it goes above that? I have never seen it happen, but I would not know who to call."

Respondents were asked whether they had submitted a maintenance request in the past three months, and if so, how long it took for the issue to be addressed.

- 22 staff said they had submitted at least one maintenance request.
- Of those, 9 said the issue was fixed within a week.
- 7 said it took between one and two weeks.
- 4 said it took more than two weeks.
- 2 said the issue was still outstanding at the time of the survey.

One respondent commented: "I put in a request for the fan in the freezer anteroom in early January. It is still not fixed. The motor whines and I worry it will stop completely." Another wrote: "The tap in the wash bay drips. I reported it before Christmas and it got fixed in the second week of January, so that was okay."

A few staff noted that they were not sure how to check the status of a maintenance request once it had been submitted. One comment read: "I hand my form to the supervisor and I never hear anything back. It would be good to know if it has been logged properly."

**Section 7: Training and Procedures**

This section asked staff about their familiarity with standard operating procedures, particularly those related to cold-chain integrity and equipment handling.

When asked about the Cold Chain Integrity Policy, 14 respondents said they were "very familiar" with it, 12 said "somewhat familiar," and 6 said they were "not very familiar." A few comments suggested that refresher training would be useful, especially for staff who had joined in the past year.

One respondent wrote: "I came in October and I got shown the chiller once. I know the basics but I would not feel confident handling a temperature excursion on my own." Another comment said: "The SOP for loading the truck is clear, but the one for the dock leveller is outdated. It does not mention the new safety gate."

There were also a few comments about the temperature log sheet near the chiller door. Several staff said that the sheet is sometimes not filled in, particularly on the weekend shift, and that they were unsure whose responsibility it was to check it.

**Section 8: General Comments**

The final section of the survey gave staff the opportunity to provide any other comments. The responses covered a range of topics, including workload, communication, and the upcoming Hobart Show Day public holiday.

On workload, one respondent wrote: "We have been short staffed on the afternoon shift for three weeks. Everyone is doing double duty and it is starting to show." Another comment said: "The morning crew is fine, but the afternoon crew is always behind because the dock gets busy after lunch."

On communication, a few staff mentioned that they would like more regular updates from the shift supervisor. One comment read: "We only hear about changes when something goes wrong. It would be good to have a quick huddle at the start of the shift, even if it is just five minutes."

One respondent raised a concern about the upcoming Hobart Show Day public holiday, noting that the roster had not been published yet and that staff were unsure whether they would be working. Another comment mentioned that the break room gets warm during the afternoon and suggested installing a second fan.

A handful of responses were positive. One staff member wrote: "The team is good and we look after each other. The new reach truck is much easier to drive than the old one." Another said: "I have been here for six years and the place has improved a lot. The chiller is reliable and we rarely have issues with the temperature."

**Section 9: Summary of Key Findings**

The survey responses indicate that staff are generally satisfied with the overall operation of the warehouse, but there are several areas where improvements could be made. The most frequently mentioned issues were:

1. The dock leveller at bay 2, which has been reported as faulty by multiple staff members.
2. The scratched screen on the handheld temperature probe.
3. The flickering light near bay 4 in the packing area.
4. The lack of visibility of temperature readouts from the chiller.
5. Uncertainty about the procedure for reporting a temperature excursion.
6. Inconsistent completion of the temperature log sheet, particularly on weekends.
7. Delays in addressing some maintenance requests.
8. A desire for more regular communication from the shift supervisor.

A final comment in this area said: "I do not have any complaints about the co‑op. They are better than the last supplier. I just hope we do not go back to the old arrangement."

**Section 11: Training and Skill Development**

When asked about training, the majority of respondents (34 out of 47) said they had received enough training to do their job safely. However, several comments indicated a desire for more specific training.

One respondent wrote: "I would like to do a refresher on the reach truck. I have not driven one for a while and I am not confident."

Another said: "The new handheld temp probe is good, but the screen is scratched and hard to read in the light. I have asked for a replacement twice. It would be good if we could have a short session on how to use the probe properly, because some staff do not know how to log the readings."

A third comment mentioned: "I have been here for two years and I have never been shown how to do the temperature excursion report. I know we are supposed to fill it in, but I do not know where the forms are."

One respondent suggested: "It would be good to have a training session on the chiller alarms. I do not know what to do if the alarm goes off at night."

Another comment said: "The new staff are not trained properly on the dock. They do not know how to stack the pallets and they leave gaps. We need a proper induction."

A further response noted: "I would like to learn how to use the computer system for the inventory. I am only on the dock, but it would help if I could check the stock levels myself."

One respondent wrote: "The training is fine, but we never get a follow‑up. I did the first aid course three years ago and I have not done a refresher since."

**Section 12: General Comments and Suggestions**

The final section of the survey invited any other comments. Responses varied widely.

One respondent wrote: "The coffee machine in the break room has been broken for two weeks. I have reported it, but nothing has happened. It is a small thing, but it makes a difference."

Another said: "The car park is too small. People park on the grass and it gets muddy in the rain. We need more spaces or a better layout."

A third comment read: "The uniform is not warm enough for the chiller. I have to wear my own jumper underneath and it is not the right colour. Can we get better jackets?"

One respondent noted: "The toilet on the dock is out of order again. It has been like that for a month. We have to walk all the way to the front office."

Another comment said: "I appreciate that we get paid on time and the shifts are regular. It is a good place to work overall."

documents.title: Warehouse Staff Survey – Perceptions and Suggestions
documents.content:
**Warehouse Staff Survey – Perceptions and Suggestions (continued)**

**Section 13: Safety and Communication**

When asked about safety in the workplace, most respondents rated the overall conditions as acceptable, though several raised specific concerns about the dock area and the chiller.

One respondent commented: "The floor near the freezer door is always wet. I have slipped twice this month. We need a mat or something to dry it."

Another said: "The safety talk at the start of shift is good, but it is always the same. We hear the same thing every day and people stop listening."

A third response read: "The first aid kit on the dock is never full. I checked it last week and there was no bandage left. The checklist says it is checked every Monday, but I am not sure who does it."

One respondent noted: "The forklift drivers are careful, but the new guy on the afternoon shift drives too fast. I have told the supervisor twice, but nothing has been done."

Another comment said: "We had a good safety meeting last month about the cold chain. It was useful to go over the temperature rules again. We should do that more often."

On communication, responses were mixed. Several staff said they felt informed about shift changes, but many wanted more notice.

One respondent wrote: "The roster comes out on Friday afternoon for the next week. It is hard to plan anything. Can we get it earlier?"

Another said: "The supervisors are good at telling us what to do, but nobody tells us why. It would help to know the bigger picture."

A third comment read: "I found out about the new pallet racking from a mate on the other shift. Nobody told us in a meeting. It would be good to hear it from the boss."

One respondent noted: "The noticeboard near the time clock is out of date. There is still a notice about the Christmas party. We need someone to keep it current."

Another said: "I like the morning huddle. It is short and we get the important stuff. But sometimes it is too loud near the dock to hear."

**Section 14: Morale and Workplace Culture**

Responses on morale were generally positive, with several staff commenting that they felt part of a team. However, a few raised concerns about fairness and recognition.

One respondent wrote: "The crew on the day shift gets along well. We help each other out. That is why I stay."

Another said: "The supervisors say thanks when we do a good job, but it does not go further than that. There is no bonus or even a mention in the newsletter."

A third comment read: "Some people get the easy jobs every day. It is the same few who always get the nice work and the rest of us do the hard stuff. It does not feel fair."

One respondent noted: "The last few months have been busy with the new season. Everyone is tired, but we are pulling together. A bit of overtime would help."

Another said: "I do not mind the work, but the music in the packing area is too loud. Some of us like it quiet. Can we have a vote?"

One respondent wrote: "The staff are good. The job is fine. It is just the little things that could be better, like the break room and the toilets."

A further comment read: "I have been here for three years and I have never had a performance review. I do not know if I am doing well or not. It would be good to know."

One respondent said: "The afternoon shift is always short staffed. I have mentioned this before, but nothing has changed. We need at least two more people."

**Section 15: Additional Comments**

The final open section of the survey gave staff the chance to add anything not covered elsewhere. Many responses repeated earlier themes, but a few new points emerged.

One respondent wrote: "The delivery drivers from the transport company are sometimes rude. They do not wait for us to check the load and they leave the dock in a hurry. It makes our job harder."

Another said: "The radio on the dock is broken. We use it to call the office when we need a hand. It has been off for a week. Can we get it fixed?"

A third comment read: "I would like to see more variety in the work. I have been on the same station for six months. It gets boring."

documents.title: Audit Debrief Facilitator Notes
documents.content:
- Dock apron temperature was logged at 14.2°C at 07:40, which is within the 15°C maximum for ambient receiving, but only just. The team noted the door seals on bay 2 are showing wear and there was a visible gap at the bottom corner. This was flagged as a risk for warmer weather.
- Two pallets of citrus arrived without a temperature recorder in the pallet. The carrier's temp log showed the trailer at 6.1°C on arrival, but there was no continuous record for the journey. QA accepted the load but noted it as a repeat issue with that carrier.
- A minor paperwork hold-up: three cartons on one delivery had a use-by date that didn't match the packing slip. Warehouse staff caught it before the pallet was put away. The supplier was contacted and the discrepancy was resolved – the cartons were accepted on the basis of the supplier's email confirmation, but QA wants this logged in the supplier performance tracker.

Action items from this section:

- Bay 2 door seals: raise a maintenance request this week. Owner: shift supervisor (Alan P.). Due: 21 Feb.
- Carrier with missing temp recorders: QA to send a formal notice to the transport manager. Owner: David. Due: 18 Feb.

---

**09:50 – Cold store storage zones**

The team reviewed the storage zone checks from yesterday arvo. General consensus was that the store was holding temperature well, but there were a few observations:

- Chiller 1 (dairy/produce) held between 1.8°C and 3.4°C across the 24-hour log. The upper reading was at 15:20 on 14 Feb, which was around the time the dock door was open for a large delivery. No product was affected, but the team agreed that door discipline needs a refresher – the dock manager said the door was open for about 12 minutes, which is longer than the 10-minute SOP limit.
- Freezer 2 (frozen lines) stayed between -21.5°C and -19.8°C. All good. One data logger was reading 0.4°C higher than the probe check, so the logger was swapped out and sent for calibration. This is noted as a follow-up – see the action list below.
- The team noticed that two pallets in the staging lane near the dispatch door had been sitting for longer than the 30-minute staging limit. The pallets were from yesterday's late dispatch and had been left overnight by mistake. They were moved back into the chiller this morning. No temperature breach was recorded on the pallet loggers, but this was flagged as a process gap – there's no clear handover between the afternoon dispatch team and the night crew about staged pallets.

Action items:

- Door discipline refresher: supervisor to run a 10-minute toolbox talk with receiving and dispatch teams. Owner: Alan P. Due: 20 Feb.
- Calibration of data logger FL-114: send to external lab. Owner: QA tech (M. Chen). Due: 24 Feb.
- Staging handover process: review the end-of-shift checklist and add a step for clearing staged pallets. Owner: David. Due: 28 Feb.

---

**10:10 – Transport and carrier handover**

Discussion moved to the transport side. The QA team had observed three carrier drop-offs and one pick-up during the audit window.

- The first carrier (Hobart-based) arrived with the trailer at 5.9°C for a chilled load. The driver's paperwork was in order and the trailer door seals were intact. Good.
- The second carrier (from Launceston) arrived 25 minutes late. The trailer was at 6.8°C, which is within the 7°C limit for chilled, but the driver didn't have a signed copy of the cold chain checklist. The driver called his depot and got a copy emailed through, so the paperwork was completed on site. QA noted this as a minor non-conformance – the checklist should be signed before departure.
- The pick-up was an export order of frozen berries. The trailer was pre-cooled to -22.1°C before loading, and the load was transferred in 18 minutes. All good. The QA team noted that the carrier's temperature recorder was placed near the door rather than in the centre of the load, which is a minor deviation from the recommended placement. Not a failure, but worth mentioning to the carrier.

**10:45 – Internal QA team debrief (continued)**

The group reviewed the audit findings from the 14th. David opened by summarising the overall picture: the site is generally in good shape, but there are recurring themes around handovers, documentation discipline, and temperature probe placement. He reminded everyone that the Quality Assurance Unit conducted_audit 2025-02-14 date. Record status: historical. and that the full written report would be circulated by the end of next week.

We went through the remaining audit observations one by one.

**Chiller room 2 – door seal and floor drain**

- Door seal on the west entrance has a visible gap at the bottom corner, roughly 30mm. Cold air loss is minor but the seal should be replaced. John from maintenance was already aware – he'd flagged it in the work order system last week. Status: work order #4821 open, parts ordered.
- Floor drain near the blast freezer entrance was dry. QA noted this is a hygiene issue – the trap needs water to maintain the seal. The cleaning contractor has been reminded twice before. John suggested a weekly check be added to the maintenance schedule rather than relying on the cleaning crew. Action: John to propose the schedule change to Alan by 21 Feb.

**Freezer 3 – evaporator fan noise**

- One of the evaporator fans in Freezer 3 is noisy. It's been like that for a few weeks according to the night crew. QA measured the temperature – it's holding at -23.5°C, so no product risk at this stage. But the fan bearing is likely wearing out. John has ordered a replacement motor and will schedule the swap for the next maintenance window. Status: planned, not urgent. Action: John to confirm the date with David by 19 Feb.

**Receiving dock – pallet jack**

- The pallet jack used on the receiving dock has a worn left wheel. It's still usable but it's hard to steer when loaded. The night crew mentioned it in their handover notes a couple of times. QA didn't formally record this as a finding – it's more of a maintenance observation. John said he'd check whether the wheel is a standard part or needs to be ordered. Action: John to check and report back by 18 Feb.

**Break room – hygiene**

- The break room fridge was noted as being overdue for a clean. There were a few old containers with no names on them. This is a housekeeping issue, not a food safety issue for the warehouse, but QA asked the shift supervisors to remind staff about the Friday clean-up roster. Action: supervisors to include in the next team huddle.

**Documentation – goods receipt records**

- QA sampled 12 goods receipt records from the last month. Two of them had the receiving time written in pen over a printed time – the handwriting made it hard to tell if it was 07:35 or 07:55. Not a big deal, but QA noted that all fields should be filled in electronically or the printed copy should be legible. The receiving team lead said they'd mention it at the next toolbox talk.

**Temperature probe placement – carrier pick-up**

- This came up again during the transport discussion. The frozen berry pick-up had the carrier's temperature recorder near the door. The recommended placement is the centre of the load. David noted that we should raise this with the carrier's dispatch office directly, not just the driver. Action: David to send an email to the carrier's cold chain contact by 20 Feb.

**General discussion – what's working well**

- The group agreed that the pre-cooling procedure for export loads is working well. The 18-minute transfer time for the berry pick-up was good.
- The pallet logger data from the staging incident was clean – no temperature breach recorded. That's a positive, even though the process gap was flagged.
- The receiving team's use of the dock scheduling sheet has improved – fewer trucks waiting this month compared to the last audit.

**Open questions / uncertainties**

- The staging incident – we don't know how long the pallets were sitting out. The night crew log shows they were discovered at 05:40, but the dispatch team's last entry was 22:15. So worst case is about 7.5 hours, but it could have been less. The pallet loggers didn't record a breach, so the product is fine. The process fix is the priority.
- The second carrier's missing checklist – the driver said it was signed electronically but he didn't have a printed copy. The depot emailed it through. We're taking that as a minor conformance issue, not a systemic problem. But David asked the QA team to keep an eye on whether this carrier has repeat issues.
- The fan in Freezer 3 – no confirmed timeline for the replacement motor delivery. John will chase it up.

**General discussion – other observations (cont.)**

- David noted that the audit itself ran about 40 minutes over schedule because of the extra time spent in the freezer area. He suggested that future audits block out a little more time for the cold storage walkthrough, or split it into two shorter visits. No decision made – just a note for the next planning session.

- Maria from the night shift mentioned during the debrief that the handover log at the end of the dock has been filling up with notes that are more about "who did what" rather than "what still needs doing." She said it makes the start of shift slower because people have to read through everything to find the open items. The group agreed this is worth tidying up, but it wasn't clear who should own it. David said he would mention it to the shift supervisors and see if they want to change the format. No action assigned yet.

- There was a short discussion about the temperature probe calibration stickers. A few probes in the chiller area have stickers that are due to expire in March. The calibration contractor is booked for the first week of March, so this should be fine, but John said he would double-check the booking is still confirmed.

- The QA team observed that the new electronic temperature log system is working well overall, but there have been a couple of instances where the time stamp on the log didn't match the time on the clock in the office. The clocks are supposed to sync automatically, but one of them is clearly not syncing. John said he would check the office clock settings when he is back on site Monday. This is a minor issue but it could cause confusion if anyone is comparing logs.

- A question came up about whether the staging area handover procedure note should include a section on what to do when a pallet has to be left overnight in the staging area. The QA team said they would include that in the draft, and they will check with the night crew about how often this actually happens. The draft is still due 24 Feb.

- David mentioned that he had received a call from the transport manager about the carrier's recorder placement issue. The carrier had called the transport manager directly rather than going through David or the QA team. David said he would follow up with the transport manager on Monday to make sure the communication goes through the right channel next time. No action item – just an observation.

- One of the auditors noted that the signage on the freezer doors is looking a bit faded, and the "Keep Closed" sign on Freezer 2 is peeling at the corner. Not urgent, but worth replacing. John said he would order new signs with the next supplies order. No date given.

- The group briefly touched on the upcoming Hobart Show Day public holiday. The warehouse will be operating with a reduced crew, and the receiving dock will be closed. David asked whether the freezer temperature checks would still run on the holiday. John confirmed that the QA team has a roster for public holidays and the checks will still happen, but they will be done by the on-call person rather than the usual QA staff. The roster is already in place.

- There was some discussion about the audit report template. The QA admin noted that the template does not currently have a field for the audit checklist version, which makes it hard to tell which version of the checklist was used for a particular audit. This was raised earlier in the session and an action was already assigned (due 20 Feb), but it came up again in general discussion because another auditor had the same question. No change to the existing action.

- A comment was made about the condition of the pallets in the staging area. Some of the wooden pallets are showing signs of wear and a couple have cracked boards. The warehouse supervisor was not at the debrief, so David said he would pass the comment along. No action assigned.

---

**Open questions / uncertainties**

- Whether the electronic dock scheduling sheet trial will start on time, given that John still needs to coordinate with the receiving team lead. John said he would confirm the dates by 1 Mar.
